candidateRows: The biological orientation of pain and pleasure is more expected on naturalism than on theism and therefore evidentially favors naturalism.
This is the first of three independent comparisons offered to establish that facts about suffering count as evidence for naturalism over theism.
Justin argues that naturalism predicts biologically useful pain and pleasure directly, whereas theism gives stronger reason to expect their orientation toward moral purposes.
The prevalence of languishing among sentient beings fits naturalism better than theism and consequently supplies evidence favoring naturalism.
This is the second principal evidential comparison in the opening case, addressing the distribution of flourishing and languishing across sentient life.
Justin contrasts widespread competition, deprivation, predation, and disease with the flourishing expected from a perfectly loving and powerful creator.
The existence of horrendous evils is substantially less surprising on naturalism than on theism and thus counts in favor of naturalism.
This is the third principal evidential comparison and directly applies divine empathy and the availability of relationship with God to horrendous suffering.
Justin argues that indifferent natural forces readily permit horrendous harms, while an omniscient, compassionate God would strongly oppose harms unnecessary for intimacy with God.
Justin has not established that naturalism itself predicts biological pain, widespread languishing, or horrendous evil better than theism.
The move attacks the naturalistic likelihood side of every evidential comparison, which is essential to denying that the cited facts favor naturalism.
Justin's claim that naturalism predicts all three cited classes of suffering better than theism.

Cameron challenges the analogy supporting biological utility and argues that evolutionary processes or harmful tendencies either belong to shared background knowledge or remain unexplained by naturalism.
A soul-building theodicy can make significant suffering at least as probable on theism as on naturalism by enabling the greatest love-manifesting virtues.
This is Cameron's central positive account for raising the probability of suffering on theism and neutralizing Justin's likelihood comparisons.
Justin's argument that the observed kinds and distribution of suffering are substantially less expected on theism.
Cameron argues that suffering enables virtues such as courage, compassion, sacrifice, and forgiveness, can be integrated into lives made better as wholes, and may be defeated eschatologically.
Skeptical theism blocks the inference from naturalism's prediction of suffering to evidential support over theism because theism's relevant predictions are unknowable.
This supplies an independent defeater to Justin's comparative argument even if the naturalistic likelihood claim succeeds and the soul-building account fails.
Justin's inference that greater expectedness of suffering on naturalism entails confirmation of naturalism over theism.
Cameron invokes the epistemic gap between humans and divinity, possible unknown or incomprehensibly complex goods, and agnosticism about theism's probability for the observed data.
The biological-purpose inference for pain and pleasure is a legitimate defeasible induction, and Cameron's compressor analogy does not undermine it.
The move defends the inferential foundation of Justin's first evidential argument against Cameron's principal objection to naturalistic prediction.
Cameron's objection that inferring the biological function of pain and pleasure resembles a faulty compressor inference.
Justin argues that if every other relevant mechanical component served propulsion, inferring that an unknown component did likewise would be reasonable though defeasible.
Evolution can remain in the background knowledge without entailing the observed imbalance of flourishing and languishing, which still fits naturalism better.
This correction preserves the second opening argument after Cameron's claim that evolutionary background knowledge would make every hypothesis predict the data.
Cameron's contention that including evolutionary processes in the background makes theism predict the languishing data too.
Justin narrows evolution to common descent and transgenerational genetic change, noting that these could obtain under theism even if widespread languishing did not.
Naturalism makes horrendous conduct and suffering less surprising because morally blind forces need not respect the psychological limits of persons.
The move directly repairs the naturalistic-likelihood component of Justin's third argument and contrasts blind natural causation with theistic expectations.
Cameron's demand for an explanation of why naturalism predicts that people act horribly or undergo horrendous suffering.
Justin says the relevant comparison concerns relative surprise: horrendous experiences puzzle observers with theistic assumptions but accord with indifferent natural forces.
Soul-building does not neutralize the evidential force of flourishing, languishing, and horrendous evil because its scope and available alternatives leave those facts more surprising on theism.
This move directly defends two of Schieber's principal evidential arguments by challenging both the coverage and moral adequacy of the proposed theodicy.
Cameron Bertuzzi's claim that soul-building makes the relevant suffering approximately as expected on theism as on naturalism.

After challenging soul-building concerning biologically oriented pain, Schieber argues that it neglects most sentient life, that God has less harmful means of moral formation, and that horrendous evil is destructive rather than constructive.

Skeptical theism cannot erase the known evidential reasons against divine permission by appealing to unknown reasons, because unknown considerations could support prevention just as readily as permission.
The move targets the principal fallback defense offered against comparative evidential reasoning and explains why epistemic uncertainty does not favor theism.
Cameron Bertuzzi's skeptical-theist contention that human inability to identify God's reasons prevents evil from counting against theism.

Schieber grants that unknown divine reasons may exist but argues that equally unknown reasons may oppose permission, leaving unknown considerations balanced while the accessible reasons retain their evidential effect.
The naturalistic inference from the biological orientation of other bodily systems to the biological orientation of pain and pleasure remains unsupported and faces a plausible moral-role alternative.
This move attacks the comparative likelihood premise required for the pain-and-pleasure evidence to favor naturalism and extends the objection to the background assumptions used for the other data.
Justin Schieber's claim that the biological functions of other organic systems support a parallel expectation about pain and pleasure under naturalism.

Bertuzzi argues that defeasibility alone does not establish a good inference, proposes that pain and pleasure may primarily serve moral roles, and says selective background knowledge does not generate naturalistic predictions of the disputed facts.
Soul-building can accommodate biologically oriented pain, animal suffering, transformative hardship, and horrendous evil while also supporting a comparative fine-tuning case for theism.
This is the principal positive defense of the soul-building theodicy, addressing each major evidential category and claiming that the overall pattern may favor theism.
Justin Schieber's objections that soul-building poorly predicts biologically oriented pain, nonhuman suffering, and permanently destructive horrendous evil.

Bertuzzi argues that stronger moral conditioning could undermine freedom and virtue, extends eventual defeat and transformation to sentient animals, disputes dreams as an equivalent substitute, denies evidence of permanent soul destruction, and invokes fine-tuning.
Skeptical theism recommends agnosticism about theism's probability for evil rather than an appeal to favorable unknown reasons, so limited known data cannot defeat that agnosticism.
The move defends the debate's main epistemic undercutting strategy and connects it directly to the conclusion that evil does not favor naturalism over theism.
Justin Schieber's argument that unknown reasons balance out and therefore known reasons may still establish evil as evidence favoring naturalism.

Using a population-sampling analogy, Bertuzzi distinguishes agnosticism from reliance on hidden justifications and argues that a small, potentially unrepresentative body of information cannot warrant the comparative probability judgment Schieber needs.
The biological orientation of pain and pleasure favors naturalism because Cameron's objections neither undermine the original analogy nor address the degree of biological versus moral orientation.
This move restores Schieber's first principal evidential comparison by defending its analogical basis and distinguishing moral relevance from predominant functional orientation.
Cameron Bertuzzi's compressor analogy and alternative hypothesis that pain and pleasure may play primarily moral rather than biological roles.

Schieber says Cameron offers no substantive objection to the organic-systems analogy and confuses pain's intrinsic moral significance with how strongly pain and pleasure are functionally directed toward biological or moral outcomes.

Cameron's soul-building account fails to predict the observed proportions of flourishing and languishing, and its appeals to dreams, eventual defeat, and fine-tuning do not answer the evidential burden.
The move defends Schieber's remaining major evil evidence by challenging the specificity, moral justification, and comparative relevance of Cameron's theodicy.
Cameron Bertuzzi's extension of soul-building to animals, rejection of dream-based alternatives, eventual-defeat account, and fine-tuning argument from evil.

Schieber argues that animal heaven is too coarse-grained to explain observed proportions, transformative experiences need not be deceptive, later compensation does not justify permission, an afterlife is auxiliary, and fine-tuning does not discharge Cameron's burden.
Limited evidence may still favor a probabilistic hypothesis, so skeptical theism's agnosticism about theism does not prevent naturalism from outperforming it on the observed evil data.
This directly resolves the debate's central comparative issue by arguing that uncertainty about one hypothesis does not erase the predictive advantage of its rival.
Cameron Bertuzzi's population-sampling analogy for remaining agnostic when available observations may not represent the larger unknown domain.

Schieber argues that a matching local sample gives some support even under substantial uncertainty, contrasts a predictive hypothesis with an unrelated agnostic one, and concludes that naturalism predicts his evil data better than skeptical theism.
Schieber has not established that naturalism predicts the evil data because his biological analogy and treatment of background knowledge remain unsupported or internally unstable.
This closing move attacks the naturalistic likelihood side of every comparative inference, which is necessary before any evil data can confirm naturalism over theism.
Justin Schieber's closing defense of his biological analogy and his claim that Cameron's old-evidence and background-knowledge objections merely poison the well.

Bertuzzi says a defeasible inference must still be shown good, maintains that his moral-role alternative can be adjusted to comparative degrees, and argues that Schieber's permissive account of background knowledge allows specifications that equalize the hypotheses.

Soul-building leaves the evil data at least as expected on theism as on naturalism because suffering enables moral growth, horrendous evil belongs to a valuable whole, and fine-tuning offsets Schieber's evidence.
This closing synthesis defends the theistic predictive account across all three categories of evil and asserts that the total evidence does not comparatively confirm naturalism.
Justin Schieber's closing claims that soul-building fails to predict languishing, confuses compensation with justification, and gains no help from fine-tuning.

Bertuzzi reiterates that naturalism lacks precise predictions, treats resource deprivation as an opportunity for sacrifice and communal growth, distinguishes integration from mere compensation, makes an afterlife integral to his narrative, and invokes fine-tuning to neutralize the comparison.
Even if evil is likely given naturalism, skeptical-theist agnosticism about its probability given theism blocks the inference that evil confirms naturalism over theism.
This directly defends the skeptical-theism argument against the claimed comparative advantage of naturalism and addresses the motion's core probabilistic inference.
Justin's claim that skeptical theism performs poorly relative to naturalism and cannot neutralize evil's evidential force.

After addressing the earlier fine-tuning exchange, Cameron distinguishes an epistemological thesis from an ontological prediction and argues that likelihood on naturalism alone does not establish comparative confirmation.
Taken together, the soul-building, fine-tuning, and skeptical-theism arguments defeat the probabilistic problem of evil.
The closing synthesis states the cumulative conclusion of the pro side and expressly connects all three defenses to the probabilistic problem of evil.
Justin's overall probabilistic case that facts about evil and suffering favor naturalism over theism.
Cameron closes by combining his first two arguments against Justin's probabilistic case and maintaining that skeptical-theist agnosticism also survived the debate.
